definitions.simple: A section of a protein that can often fold and perform a distinct function.
definitions.scientific: A protein domain is a compact structural or functional unit within a polypeptide, often capable of semi-independent folding and reused across unrelated protein architectures.

article.heading: A Functional Region Inside a Larger Chain
paragraphs: Many proteins contain recognizable regions called domains. A domain often forms a relatively compact unit within a polypeptide and may have its own binding or catalytic role. Some domains fold to a useful structure when isolated, while others depend more strongly on neighboring regions.

A protein can combine several domains in one chain. This allows one part to recognize a signal or partner while another part performs chemistry or interacts with a membrane. A domain is larger and more independently organized than a short recurring sequence or structural motif.

article.heading: Why Structural Databases Contain Domains
paragraphs: An experimental structure may cover only one domain of a full-length protein because the rest was too flexible, difficult to prepare, or not part of the experiment. A deposited domain is still useful scientific evidence about that region, but it is not equivalent to a measured structure of the entire protein.
When a CellSimulator structure has a domain in its title, treat its atomic coordinates as a view of that portion, not necessarily the complete native protein or its assembly with partners.
